title: Snakebite envenoming (WHO)
subject: toxicology
summary: Reassure, immobilise and transport without cutting, sucking or tight tourniquets. Give IV antivenom (no skin test) for systemic or severe local envenoming, the same dose for children, repeat by 20WBCT and clinical response, try atropine-neostigmine in neurotoxicity, and treat antivenom anaphylaxis with IM adrenaline.

sections.title: First aid and arrival
items: Reassure the victim (many bites are dry bites and severe envenoming usually evolves slowly). Lay them down, ideally in the recovery position on the left side, and splint or sling the bitten limb; any movement, even walking or undressing, speeds venom spread.
Unless an elapid bite can confidently be excluded, WHO SEARO recommends pressure-pad immobilisation over the bite site, preferred to pressure bandaging, which needs long elastic bandages and skill.

Do not make incisions, suck the wound, apply snake stones, herbs, chemicals, ice or electric shock, or tie tight (arterial) tourniquets. Do not try to kill the snake; a phone photograph helps identification.
Release existing tight bands only in hospital once resuscitation facilities are ready and antivenom has been started, because release can cause sudden deterioration.
On arrival: rapid assessment and resuscitation (airway, breathing, circulation), IV access, oxygen; avoid IM injections and arterial punctures in patients who may be coagulopathic.

sections.title: Clinical syndromes
items: Local envenoming: pain, swelling, blistering, bruising, tender enlarged regional lymph nodes and necrosis (cobras, vipers).

Haemotoxic (vipers such as Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper): spontaneous bleeding from gums, bite site, old wounds or into urine, incoagulable blood, shock and AKI; Russell's viper can also cause acute pituitary and adrenal insufficiency.

Neurotoxic (cobras, kraits): ptosis, external ophthalmoplegia, difficulty swallowing and speaking, neck weakness ('broken neck sign'), paradoxical breathing and respiratory paralysis. Krait bites are often painless, at night in people sleeping on the floor, with abdominal pain.
Myotoxic (sea snakes, some kraits): muscle pain and dark urine from rhabdomyolysis, with hyperkalaemia and AKI.
Pregnancy: watch for antepartum or postpartum haemorrhage, preterm labour and fetal distress or death.

sections.title: 20WBCT and laboratory tests
items: 20-minute whole blood clotting test: put 2 mL of fresh venous blood in a new, clean, dry, ordinary glass vessel, leave it undisturbed for 20 minutes at room temperature, then tip once. Blood still liquid means venom-induced consumption coagulopathy; in South-East Asia this indicates a viper and excludes an elapid.
Plastic tubes or glass washed with detergent give false non-clotting results; if in doubt repeat in duplicate with a healthy control's blood.
Where available: INR (1.2 or more is abnormal), aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer or fibrin degradation products; bedside INR and D-dimer devices are unreliable in snakebite.

Also blood count, platelets and smear (fragmented red cells), creatinine, urea, potassium, CK and aminotransferases, urine dipstick for blood or myoglobin, ECG, and bedside measures of ventilatory capacity.
Repeat the 20WBCT 6 hours after each antivenom dose and at intervals thereafter, because viper envenoming can recur 24 to 48 hours after an initial response.

sections.title: Antivenom: indications and administration
items: Systemic envenoming: spontaneous bleeding, non-clotting 20WBCT, INR above 1.2 or prothrombin time more than 4 to 5 seconds above control, thrombocytopenia, neurotoxic signs, hypotension, shock, arrhythmia or abnormal ECG, AKI, or haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria.

Local envenoming: swelling of more than half the bitten limb within 48 hours (without a tourniquet), swelling after bites on digits, rapid extension beyond the wrist or ankle within a few hours of a hand or foot bite, or tender enlarged draining lymph nodes.

Give antivenom as soon as it is indicated and as long as coagulopathy persists, even days after the bite; it rarely prevents local necrosis unless given within a few hours. Do not give it for bites without envenoming.
Give IV only: slow push at no more than 2 mL/min, or infusion diluted in about 5 mL/kg of isotonic fluid over 30 to 60 minutes. Never inject at the bite site; IM only if nobody can give IV.
Do not perform skin or conjunctival hypersensitivity tests; they do not predict reactions. Keep adrenaline drawn up and observe closely for at least 1 hour after starting.
Use only an antivenom whose range covers the species; regional polyvalent antivenoms may not cover hump-nosed pit vipers, sea snakes or some cobras (for example Naja kaouthia).

sections.title: Antivenom dose and repeat dosing
items: Initial dose is empirical; a high loading dose is more logical than repeated small doses. WHO SEARO guide for Indian polyvalent antivenom: Russell's viper and common krait 100 mL (about 10 vials); Indian cobra and saw-scaled viper 50 mL (about 5 vials).
Children must receive exactly the same dose as adults (snakes inject the same amount of venom); the same applies in pregnancy.
Repeat the initial dose if blood remains incoagulable 6 hours after the previous dose, within 1 to 2 hours if brisk bleeding continues, and after 1 hour if neurotoxic or cardiovascular signs worsen.
Further antivenom has no proven value once a paralysed patient is being ventilated; continue ventilation and supportive care.
No suitable antivenom: treat conservatively with assisted ventilation, anticholinesterases for neurotoxicity, blood products for bleeding, vasopressors for shock and dialysis for AKI.

sections.title: Antivenom reactions
items: WHO SEARO recommends prophylactic adrenaline 0.25 mg SC (0.25 mL of 1 mg/mL; children 0.005 mL/kg) just before antivenom, except in older patients with suspected cerebrovascular disease or when the antivenom has a proven reaction rate below 5%. Antihistamines, hydrocortisone and slow infusion do not prevent reactions.

Early anaphylactic reaction (itching, urticaria, tachycardia, restlessness, bronchospasm, hypotension): pause antivenom and give adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (children 0.01 mg/kg) into the thigh, repeated every 5 to 10 minutes if needed.

After adrenaline give chlorphenamine 10 mg IV (children 0.2 mg/kg) and hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (children 2 mg/kg); for shock lay flat with legs raised and give 1 to 2 L of 0.9% saline, then an adrenaline infusion if needed. Resume antivenom cautiously once recovered.
Pyrogenic reaction (rigors, fever within 1 to 2 hours): cooling, paracetamol and IV fluids.
Serum sickness (1 to 12 days later): chlorphenamine for 5 days; if no response in 24 to 48 hours, prednisolone for 5 to 7 days.

sections.title: Neurotoxicity and supportive care
items: Intubate or insert a supraglottic airway and ventilate for respiratory distress, neck weakness with shallow or paradoxical breathing, pooling secretions with loss of gag reflex, SpO2 below 90% despite high-flow oxygen, or rising PaCO2. Paralysed patients may be fully conscious: sedate them, and do not diagnose brain death.

Anticholinesterase trial in every neurotoxic patient (without delaying antivenom or intubation): atropine 0.6 mg IV (children 50 mcg/kg), then neostigmine 0.02 mg/kg IM (children 0.04 mg/kg); watch ptosis and ventilatory capacity for 30 to 60 minutes. It often works after cobra bites, rarely after krait bites.
Convincing response: maintain neostigmine 0.5 to 2.5 mg every 1 to 3 hours (maximum 10 mg in 24 hours; children 0.01 to 0.04 mg/kg every 2 to 4 hours) IM, IV or SC with atropine.

Hypotension: assess fluid responsiveness (postural change or passive leg raise), give fluids with care, then a vasopressor. Suspect acute pituitary or adrenal insufficiency after Russell's viper bite and give hydrocortisone, which can be life-saving.
AKI: monitor urine output and potassium; dialysis for hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, severe acidosis or uraemia. Give blood products only after antivenom has neutralised the venom.

Tetanus toxoid booster; antibiotics for necrotic or infected wounds; early debridement of necrotic tissue. Fasciotomy only after antivenom has corrected haemostasis, with clinical compartment syndrome and raised compartment pressure confirmed by direct measurement.

sections.title: Admission and national differences
items: Observe every snakebite with repeated clinical examination and 20WBCT, because signs of envenoming can appear late; do not discharge early.
Before discharge: explain the course, advise on avoiding bites, arrange follow-up and physiotherapy for the bitten limb, and warn about serum sickness.

India: NAPSE (2024) admits every snakebite for at least 24 hours, and MoHFW protocols set Indian polyvalent antivenom doses and schedules (including a low-dose viper infusion regimen) and a fixed atropine-neostigmine schedule. Follow the national protocol where it applies.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying antivenom to wait for a 20WBCT when there is spontaneous systemic bleeding, or withholding it for fear of reactions.
Giving antivenom for bites without envenoming, or giving children a reduced dose.
Using plastic or detergent-washed tubes for the 20WBCT.
Missing krait envenoming (painless bite, abdominal pain, then ptosis), or repeating antivenom in ventilated patients instead of supporting them.

drugs.name: Polyvalent antivenom
drugs.dose: IV slow push (no more than 2 mL/min) or infusion in 5 mL/kg isotonic fluid over 30 to 60 minutes. WHO SEARO initial guide for Indian polyvalent: 100 mL (about 10 vials) for Russell's viper or common krait; 50 mL (about 5 vials) for cobra or saw-scaled viper
drugs.notes: Same dose for children and in pregnancy. Repeat at 6 hours if blood is still incoagulable, within 1 to 2 hours for continued bleeding, after 1 hour for neurological or cardiovascular deterioration.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg/mL
drugs.dose: Prophylaxis 0.25 mg SC before antivenom (children 0.005 mL/kg); anaphylaxis 0.5 mg IM (children 0.01 mg/kg), repeat every 5 to 10 minutes
drugs.notes: Omit prophylaxis in older patients with suspected cerebrovascular disease. Safe in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Chlorphenamine
drugs.dose: 10 mg IV (children 0.2 mg/kg) after adrenaline for anaphylaxis; serum sickness 2 mg orally every 6 hours (children 0.25 mg/kg/day in divided doses) for 5 days
drugs.notes: Adjunct only; does not prevent reactions.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: 100 mg IV (children 2 mg/kg) after adrenaline in anaphylaxis
drugs.notes: Also for suspected pituitary or adrenal insufficiency after Russell's viper bite. Not for prophylaxis.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally every 6 hours (children 0.7 mg/kg/day in divided doses) for 5 to 7 days
drugs.notes: Serum sickness not responding to antihistamine within 24 to 48 hours.

drugs.name: Neostigmine
drugs.dose: Test dose 0.02 mg/kg IM (children 0.04 mg/kg) after atropine; maintenance 0.5 to 2.5 mg every 1 to 3 hours, maximum 10 mg in 24 hours (children 0.01 to 0.04 mg/kg every 2 to 4 hours)
drugs.notes: Only if the test shows a convincing response; always with atropine.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 0.6 mg IV (children 50 mcg/kg) before each neostigmine dose
